title: Google's Suncatcher Satellite Answers First Prompt From Orbit With a Haiku
excerpt: A Gemma 4 model running on a data-center-class TPU aboard Google's prototype satellite replied to a prompt from Earth — the first test of the company's plan to run AI computing in space.
body:
• Google's Project Suncatcher prototype satellite has returned its first complete AI response from orbit: a haiku written by the Gemma 4 model running on one of its onboard Tensor Processing Units.
  • The satellite, built in partnership with Planet, launched on October 1 aboard SpaceX's Transporter-18 rideshare mission carrying four Trillium-generation TPU chips.
  • Power is the binding constraint: the satellite generates up to 1 kilowatt, so only one TPU can run at a time, for roughly 20 minutes, according to TechCrunch.
  • Google will next test how the chips withstand thermal stress and radiation in orbit, ahead of two interconnected satellites planned for 2027.

Google has received the first AI response generated by one of its data-center-class chips in orbit. During a ground-station pass this week, engineers uplinked a prompt to the Project Suncatcher prototype satellite, booted up its onboard Tensor Processing Unit (TPU), and got a complete reply back on Earth: a haiku about being in space, written by the Gemma 4 open model loaded on the spacecraft.

Chief executive Sundar Pichai announced the result on October 30, calling it a "'hello world' milestone for Project Suncatcher." The response came down as the satellite passed over Svalbard, Norway, according to The Hindu BusinessLine's report of Google's announcement. The haiku read: "Blue marble below / Data streams in silent grace / Starlight feeds my core."

"After launching our prototype satellite a few weeks ago, we've now successfully sent a command up to orbit, booted up the TPU, ran the prompt, and received our first complete response back on earth - a haiku!"

— Sundar Pichai, CEO, Google

How the test worked

The satellite was built in partnership with Planet and launched on October 1 aboard SpaceX's Transporter-18 rideshare mission. In the weeks since, the team ran commissioning checks, powered up the host computer and the TPU trays, and carried out early machine-learning tests before attempting the full prompt-and-response exchange. After the haiku, the team also tested the system with space-themed limericks and with prompts asking the model to report the technical status of the satellite's systems. A Google spokesperson told TechCrunch the satellite is operating nominally.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DeSuiavml1p/

The hardware is modest by design. The prototype carries four Trillium-generation TPUs and generates up to 1 kilowatt of electricity. Because of that power budget, only one chip can run at a time, and only for about 20 minutes per session, which also complicates scheduling contact with ground stations. Google has published no performance figures for the exchange; this was a demonstration that the hardware works in orbit, not a benchmark.

Why Google wants compute in space

Project Suncatcher is Google's long-term research effort to test whether AI computing infrastructure can run in space. The rationale is energy. Satellites in low Earth orbit can sit in near-constant sunlight, and Google has said they could potentially generate up to eight times more solar power than panels on Earth. The longer-term idea is compact constellations of solar-powered satellites, each carrying TPUs and linked by free-space optical communication, handling AI workloads that on Earth require ever-larger, power-hungry data centers.

https://x.com/Google/status/2116244903155929115

Google is not the only company testing the idea. Nvidia-backed startup Starcloud flew an Nvidia H100 GPU aboard its Starcloud-1 satellite in November 2025 and used it to train a small model in space for the first time, and it has since raised hundreds of millions of dollars to scale up its orbital data-center plans.

What happens next

The next phase of the Suncatcher mission will test how the TPUs perform under thermal stress and radiation exposure over longer stretches in orbit — the two environmental risks most likely to corrupt data or kill the chips. If the hardware holds up, Google's next milestone is a pair of interconnected satellites in 2027, designed to test the high-bandwidth laser links a future constellation would need. For now, Google is explicit that Suncatcher remains a research experiment aimed at the 2030s, not a product.
